The Education

Why Most Dental Practices Leave a Significant Portion of Revenue on the Medical Insurance Side

Dental billing and medical billing operate in parallel universes dental procedures use CDT (Current Dental Terminology) codes and are submitted to dental insurance, while medical procedures use CPT codes and are submitted to medical insurance. The problem: many dental procedures are also medically billable under CPT codes to medical insurance and most dental practices never submit the medical side of the claim at all.

Sleep apnea oral appliance therapy is the clearest example. When a physician diagnoses obstructive sleep apnea with a sleep study, and a dentist fabricates and fits a mandibular advancement device, the oral appliance is a covered benefit under medical insurance specifically, HCPCS code E0486 (oral device/appliance used to reduce upper airway collapsibility, adjustable or non-adjustable). Most dental practices managing sleep apnea patients bill the patient self-pay or submit to dental insurance (where coverage is limited) missing the $800 to $2,500 medical insurance reimbursement for the E0486 device and the associated medical E/M visits.

Oral surgery for trauma, cancer reconstruction, cleft palate, and craniofacial anomalies crosses fully into medical billing territory the procedures are performed in hospital or ASC settings, use CPT codes, require medical prior authorization, and are payable by medical insurance only. An oral surgeon performing jaw reconstruction after a motor vehicle accident is performing a medical procedure that medical insurance pays for but if the practice only has dental billing infrastructure, this revenue is systematically not captured.

The Revenue Source Most Dental Practices Do Not Know Exists

The Dental-Medical Billing Crossover

The dental-medical billing crossover is the practice of correctly identifying when a dental procedure qualifies for medical insurance reimbursement and submitting that claim to the patient's medical insurance. This is not upcoding or billing manipulation it is correctly billing the right payer for the right service. Medical insurance covers procedures medically necessary to treat medical diagnoses. When a dental procedure is performed to treat a medical diagnosis, medical insurance is the correct payer.

The most common crossover categories: (1) Sleep apnea oral appliance therapy E0486 device billing plus medical E/M codes. (2) Oral and maxillofacial surgery for trauma CPT jaw reconstruction, fracture repair, soft tissue repair codes. (3) Oral surgery for cancer reconstruction implants, prosthetics, and surgical repair following oncologic resection. (4) TMJ disorder treatment intra-articular injections (CPT 20610), arthroscopy (CPT 29800), and E/M visits for TMJ management. (5) Cleft palate and craniofacial surgery CPT codes for palate repair, alveolar bone grafting, and nasal reconstruction. (6) Dental implants following trauma or cancer when implant placement is medically indicated by documented tooth loss from a medical cause.

PMEx implements a medical billing workflow alongside the practice's existing dental billing screening every patient encounter for medical crossover eligibility, submitting medical insurance claims for qualifying procedures, and building a second revenue stream from the medical side of care the practice is already delivering.
